steps.text: A triad is three notes stacked in thirds. The middle note — the third — decides the mood: major third (4 semitones) sounds bright, minor third (3 semitones) sounds darker. The fifth just anchors it.
steps.title: TRIADS

steps.text: Listen: C–E–G, a C major triad. The major third (C to E) rings close to the natural harmonic series, which is why it sounds settled and sunny.
steps.title: MAJOR

steps.text: Now A–C–E, A minor. One semitone moved — E to C is now a minor third — and the whole chord darkens. That single semitone is the difference between happy and sad in Western music.
steps.title: MINOR

steps.text: Build a G major triad on step 8: G (67), B (71), D (74). In the piano roll, click the lanes — or ask me and I'll place it. Major = root + 4 + 7 semitones.
steps.title: YOUR TURN

steps.text: Stacked thirds work because the intervals are consonant: the fifth is a 3:2 frequency ratio, the major third 5:4. Simple ratios, simple sound. Dissonance is just complex ratios — useful for tension, bad for rest.
steps.title: WHY IT WORKS
